learningGoal.source: Tell what you can see in an artwork from what its history explains, describe its composition and medium, and explain why an artwork gives a chosen view of people's lives.
learningGoal.back: Separate what you see in an artwork from what the work's history explains, describe the work's composition and materials, and explain why an artwork shows only a chosen angle of people's lives.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Images have makers, audiences and settings
read.sections.0.heading.back: A picture has its makers, viewers and place

read.sections.0.text.source:
Art history studies images and objects together with the people who made, supported, bought, and used them. An artwork's composition, or arrangement, directs attention. Its medium, or material, affects how it was made and how people experience it. Two different works connect artistic choices with work, wealth, and the ways people picture their surroundings.

Katsushika Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830–32, during Japan's Edo period. It belongs to a series called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Curving water fills the picture, while the mountain appears as a small triangle in the distance. His landscapes used indigo and imported Prussian blue, so an image of a Japanese place also connects with materials that moved across borders.

Edo-period Japan was governed by the Tokugawa military government. Growing cities and trade supported prosperous merchants and craftspeople, often called chōnin, or townspeople. Their spending helped keep a market going for pictures of actors, entertainment, and famous places. Money did not give merchants the highest official social rank. Buyers' interests mattered alongside artists' ideas and government rules. Hokusai worked within this city culture; his prints do not express everything about Japan.
read.sections.0.text.note: medium chosen as วัสดุ (not in KEY_TERMS; Thai art textbooks also say สื่อวัสดุ, but สื่อ is 'media' elsewhere on the platform). Other AAS lessons may use the same word: a reviewer should decide one. Tokugawa government as รัฐบาลทหารของตระกูลโทกูงาวะ; chōnin as โชนิน; Prussian blue as สีน้ำเงินปรัสเซีย. Reviewer: made clear that only the Prussian blue was imported (the draft could be read as indigo imported too).
read.sections.0.text.back:
Art history studies pictures and objects together with the people who made, supported, bought and used them. Composition, or the arrangement of the parts of an artwork, leads the viewer's eye. Medium, or what is used to make the work, affects how the work is made and how people perceive it. The two different works in this lesson connect artistic decisions to work, wealth and the way people pictured what was around them.

Katsushika Hokusai made The Great Wave off Kanagawa around 1830–32 in Japan's Edo period. It is in a series called 36 Views of Mount Fuji. Curling water fills the picture, while the mountain is only a small triangle far away. His landscapes used indigo, and also Prussian blue imported from abroad. So a picture of a place in Japan was also connected to materials that travelled across borders.

Japan in the Edo period was ruled by the military government of the Tokugawa family. Growing cities and trade made many merchants and artisans well off. This group was often called chōnin, or townspeople. Their spending helped the market for pictures of actors, entertainment and famous places keep going. But money did not give merchants the highest social rank as the authorities set it. Buyers' interests mattered alongside the artist's ideas and the government's rules. Hokusai worked inside this kind of city culture. His prints do not tell everything about Japan.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art history looks at objects and the people around them. Who made them? Who paid? Who used them? The composition is how the parts are arranged. It leads your eye. The medium is what a work is made of.

Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830 in Japan. Huge waves fill the picture. Mount Fuji is a small shape far away. He used a blue paint that came from Europe. So a picture of Japan also used things from far away.

At that time, military rulers governed Japan. Cities grew. Many traders and craftspeople had money. People called them townspeople. They bought pictures of actors and famous places. But money did not give them the top rank. Hokusai made prints for this city market.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Art history studies objects and the people around them. Who made it? Who paid? Who used it? Composition is the arrangement of the parts in a picture. It leads our eyes. Medium is what is used to make the work.

Hokusai made The Great Wave off Kanagawa around 1830 in Japan. A very big wave fills the picture. Mount Fuji is a small shape far away. He used a blue colour that came from Europe. So a picture of Japan also used things from far away.

At that time, military rulers governed Japan. Cities grew. Many merchants and artisans had money. People called them townspeople. They bought pictures of actors and famous places. But money did not give them the highest rank. Hokusai made prints for this city market.

read.sections.1.heading.source: How a woodblock print was made
read.sections.1.heading.back: How a woodblock print is made

read.sections.1.text.source:
This work is a woodblock print. A design is transferred to a block of wood. Areas are cut away, and the raised surface takes the ink. Paper laid over it takes the image. Colour printing uses separate blocks lined up on the same sheet. Many impressions, or printed copies, can come from the blocks.

Several specialists worked together. The designer supplied the image, a carver prepared the blocks, a printer added the colours, and a publisher ran the business. Publishers helped choose subjects and how carefully a print was made. A famous artist's name identifies one contribution within a wider world of skilled work and business.
read.sections.1.text.note: impression chosen as ฉบับพิมพ์ (not in KEY_TERMS); woodblock print ภาพพิมพ์แกะไม้; publisher ผู้จัดพิมพ์.
read.sections.1.text.back:
This work is a woodblock print. A craftsman traces the picture onto a wooden block, then carves away the parts not needed. The raised surface takes the ink. When paper is laid on top, the paper takes the picture. Colour printing uses many separate blocks lined up on one sheet of paper. The same set of blocks can print many impressions, or copies.

Several specialists worked together. The designer provided the picture, the carver prepared the blocks, the printer applied the colour, and the publisher ran the business. The publisher helped choose subjects to print and decided how finely to print. So a famous artist's name tells only part of the work, among much more craft and business.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
This picture is a woodblock print. A design is put on a block of wood. Some parts are cut away. Ink goes on the raised parts. Paper on top takes the picture. Each colour has its own block. Many copies, called impressions, come from the same blocks.

Many people made one print. An artist drew it. A carver cut the blocks. A printer added the colours. A publisher sold the prints. So a famous name is only one part of the work.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
This picture is a woodblock print. A craftsman draws the design on a wooden block, then carves some parts away. Ink sticks to the raised parts. Paper laid on top takes the picture. Each colour has its own block. One set of blocks can print many sheets. Each sheet is called an impression.

One print needs many people. The artist draws the picture. The carver makes the block. The printer applies the colour. The publisher sells the picture. So the famous name is only part of the work.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Harvesters is an oil painting on oak from 1565. Workers cut grain and rest beneath a tree. A wealthy merchant in Antwerp ordered its series of seasons for the dining room of his country house. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes the farm scene as sympathetic, but idealised for that patron.

Here the word Netherlandish describes a historical region, not the Dutch state of today. Antwerp, now in Belgium, belonged to the Low Countries, ruled by the Habsburg family. It was a centre of trade, printing, and art markets. A picture of the countryside could hang in the cultured home of someone whose wealth and daily life were in the city. Knowing this setting stops us from mistaking the patron's chosen view for the life of every farm worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers; a commissioned painting served one patron and one room. Both organise attention, but their audiences and ways of making differ. Form and historical context together help explain how each work belonged to a society.
read.sections.2.text.note: The English sentence about the word 'Netherlandish' is kept as คำว่าเนเธอร์แลนด์ ... though the Thai text never otherwise uses that word (nor does the English). Habsburg as ราชวงศ์ฮาพส์บวร์ค. grain translated as ข้าวสาลี (wheat, as in the painting) to avoid ข้าว = rice.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Harvesters is an oil painting on oak panel from 1565. In it, workers are cutting wheat and sitting resting under a tree. A wealthy Antwerp merchant commissioned this season series for the dining room of his country house. The Metropolitan Museum of Art says this farm picture looks at the workers with sympathy, but also paints them better than reality for that patron.

Here, the word Netherlands means a historical region, not today's country of the Netherlands. Antwerp, which is now in Belgium, was part of the Low Countries ruled by the Habsburg dynasty. The city was a centre of trade, printing and the art market. So a country picture could hang in the tasteful house of someone rich who lived daily life in the city. Knowing this context helps us not mistake the patron's chosen view for the life of every farm worker.

Prints are made in many copies for many buyers, but a commissioned painting is for one patron and one room. Both kinds of work are arranged to guide the viewer's attention, but their audiences and ways of being made differ. The form of the work and its historical context together explain how each work is part of a society.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Bruegel painted The Harvesters in 1565 on a wooden panel. Workers cut grain and rest under a tree. A rich trader in the city of Antwerp was its patron. He paid for it. It hung in the dining room of his country house. The museum says the scene is kind to the workers. But it is nicer than real life.

Antwerp is now in Belgium. Then it was a busy city of trade and art. So this picture of farm work hung in a rich city home. It shows his view, not the life of every worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers. A painting was made for one person and one room. Looking at the work and its context together helps us understand it.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Bruegel painted The Harvesters on a wooden panel in 1565. Workers cut wheat and rest under a tree. A rich merchant in Antwerp was the patron of this picture. He paid for it to be painted. The picture hung in the eating room of his country house. The museum says the picture looks at the workers kindly, but it also looks better than real life.

Now Antwerp is in Belgium. Then it was a busy city of trade and art. So this picture of farm work hung in a rich person's house in the city. The picture shows his view, not the life of every worker.

Prints are made in many sheets for many buyers. A painting is made for one person and one room. Looking at both the work itself and its context together helps us understand the work.

write.prompt.source: Pick Hokusai's print or Bruegel's painting. Explain how one thing you can see and one fact from its history help you understand it. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.prompt.back: Choose Hokusai's print or Bruegel's painting. Explain how one thing you see and one fact from the work's history help you understand the work. 2 or 3 sentences is enough.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: In the picture, I can see ...

write.sentenceStarters.1.back: The work's history tells us that...

write.example.source: In Hokusai's print, I can see a huge wave in front and Mount Fuji very small behind it. The history tells us that prints like this were made in many copies and sold to townspeople in Japan's growing cities. Together, these show that the picture was made to catch the eye of buyers. It does not show everything about life in Japan.
write.example.back: In Hokusai's print, I see a very big wave in front and a very small Mount Fuji behind. The work's history tells us that prints like this were made in many copies and sold to townspeople in Japan's growing cities. Put together, these show that the picture was made to catch buyers' eyes. It does not show everything about life in Japan.
